passages.happening:
Some time later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus shows himself to his disciples again (verse 1). Seven of them are together: Simon Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee and two others (verse 2). Peter says, “I am going fishing,” and the others go with him. They fish all night and catch nothing (verse 3).

At dawn Jesus is standing on the shore, but they do not know him (verse 4). “Children, do you have any fish?” he calls. “No,” they answer (verse 5). He tells them to cast the net on the right side of the boat, and they cannot haul it in for the number of fish (verse 6).

The disciple whom Jesus loved says to Peter, “It is the Lord!” Peter throws on his outer garment and jumps into the sea (verse 7). The others bring the boat in, dragging the net (verse 8). On the shore there is a charcoal fire with fish on it, and bread (verse 9). Jesus says, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught” (verse 10). Peter hauls the net ashore, full of large fish, “153, but even with so many, the net was not torn” (verse 11).

“Come, have breakfast,” Jesus says. None of them dares ask who he is. They know it is the Lord (verse 12). Jesus takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish too (verse 13). This is the third time he has appeared to the disciples since he was raised (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
John's book seemed to end at 20:31. Then this chapter begins. The book page explains in ‘Two passages, and what the old copies show’ that many scholars think chapter 21 was added in the book's final edition, and that, unlike the story of the woman caught in adultery, chapter 21 is in every surviving copy of John that has the ending. It is part of John as the church has always received it.

The Sea of Tiberias is the Sea of Galilee, named after the town Herod Antipas built on its shore in honor of the emperor Tiberius. The disciples have gone home to Galilee, and to the work they knew. Peter's ‘I am going fishing’ may be no more than a man needing something to do with his hands. Many readers also hear in it a man who does not know what else to do after failing so badly.

Luke tells of another night of empty nets, at the very start, when Jesus first called Peter and said, “From now on you will catch men” (Luke 5:4-10). Here the call is renewed in the same way. The disciples would remember.

Notice the charcoal fire. John uses that word only twice: for the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter denied Jesus (18:18), and here. Jesus has lit a fire like the one where Peter failed, and he is cooking breakfast on it.

Why 153 fish? John does not say, and people have guessed for centuries. Jerome, in the 400s, said that ancient writers on nature counted 153 kinds of fish, so the catch stood for people of every kind; but scholars who have checked the ancient writers on fish find no such exact count. Augustine noticed that 153 is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 17, and he read 17 as 10 (the commandments) and 7 (the Spirit). Others have tried codes in the letters of names. These are guesses, and none is certain. Many scholars think the simplest answer is likely: someone counted, and remembered. The point John makes plainly is that the net did not tear.
passages.ot:
The prophets used fishing as a picture of God gathering people. Jeremiah heard God say, “I will send for many fishermen” (Jeremiah 16:16), and in Ezekiel's vision of the river flowing from the temple, fishermen “will spread their nets to catch fish of many kinds” (Ezekiel 47:10). Jesus had promised to make his friends “fishers of men” (Mark 1:17).

Isaiah called the hungry to God's feast: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55:1). The risen Lord says the same thing on a beach: ‘Come, have breakfast.’
passages.hard:
Is this chapter part of John's Gospel? Yes, in every copy of John that has its ending. Many scholars think it was added when the book was finished, perhaps by the circle of disciples who speak as ‘we’ in verse 24; others think the same author added it himself. Either way, it does not change any teaching of the faith, and the church has read it as Scripture from the beginning. The book page says this plainly, without alarm.

Why did they not recognize him at first? John says it was early morning, and they were about a hundred yards out. And as with Mary at the tomb, the risen Jesus was not always known at once. When he spoke and acted, they knew him.
passages.asks: Peter went back to what he knew, and caught nothing. Then Jesus met him there, in his ordinary work, and fed him. Ask where you have gone back to old ways after a failure, and whether you expect Jesus to meet you there. And notice what the risen Lord of the world did that morning: he lit a fire and cooked breakfast for tired, hungry men who had let him down.

passages.t: Do you love Me? Feed My sheep
passages.happening:
When they have eaten, Jesus asks Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” “Yes, Lord,” he answers, “You know I love You.” Jesus says, “Feed My lambs” (verse 15).

A second time: “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord,” Peter answers, “You know I love You.” Jesus says, “Shepherd My sheep” (verse 16).

A third time: “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter is deeply hurt that Jesus asks him a third time. “Lord, You know all things,” he replies. “You know I love You.” Jesus says to him, “Feed My sheep” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Three times beside a charcoal fire, Peter had said he did not know Jesus (18:17, 25, 27). Now, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus asks him three times whether he loves him. No one at that fire could miss it. Peter is hurt by the third question because he understands it. But Jesus is not rubbing in the failure. He is giving Peter three chances to say yes, one for each no, and each time he gives him work to do.

Jesus calls him ‘Simon son of John’, the name he had before Jesus named him Peter (1:42). He has gone back to the beginning.

‘More than these’ can be read in three ways: more than these other disciples love me; more than you love these other disciples; or more than you love these things, the boat and the nets. Peter had once boasted that even if all the others fell away, he would not (Mark 14:29). Many readers think Jesus is asking gently whether he still thinks so. Notice that Peter does not compare himself with anyone now. He only says, ‘You know.’

There are two Greek words for ‘love’ in these verses, though English Bibles usually translate both as ‘love’. In Jesus' first two questions the verb is agapaō. Peter answers each time with phileō. In the third question Jesus uses phileō too.

Some readers think the difference matters. They hear agapaō as the deeper, self-giving love, and phileō as the love of friends. Peter, humbled, will only claim the lesser word, and at the third question Jesus comes down to meet him where he is.

Other readers think the two words mean the same here, and that John is simply varying his words, as he often does. They point out that John says the Father ‘loves’ the Son with agapaō in one place (3:35) and with phileō in another (5:20). John also varies his words for ‘feed’ and ‘shepherd’, ‘lambs’ and ‘sheep’, in these same verses. Scholars are divided between these views. These notes take no side. On either reading, the threefold question undoes the threefold denial.
passages.ot:
God had complained through Ezekiel about Israel's bad shepherds: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). God promised, “I will give you shepherds after My own heart” (Jeremiah 3:15). The flock belongs to God. Isaiah pictures the LORD himself as the shepherd who “gathers the lambs in His arms” (Isaiah 40:11).

Jesus is the good shepherd (10:11). Now he gives Peter his sheep to care for, but they remain ‘My sheep’. Peter later wrote to church leaders, “Be shepherds of God's flock that is among you” (1 Peter 5:2).

A psalm of a man who had failed badly prays, “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation” (Psalm 51:12). That is what happens to Peter on the shore.
passages.hard:
What did ‘Feed My sheep’ give Peter? Churches read it in different ways, as they read ‘You are Peter, and on this rock’ (Matthew 16:18). Here each is stated as its own teachers state it.

Catholic teaching sees here the risen Christ giving Peter the care of his whole flock. The First Vatican Council (1870) taught that Christ conferred on Peter alone a primacy of jurisdiction over the whole church, and it pointed to these verses: Jesus made Peter the shepherd and ruler of all his fold. The Catechism of the Catholic Church says that Christ gave Peter the keys and made him shepherd of the whole flock, citing this passage, and Catholics hold that this office continues in the bishops of Rome.

The Orthodox honour Peter, and read the scene as his restoration and his calling as a shepherd of Christ's people, but they do not accept the claim that the bishop of Rome governs the whole church.

Many Protestants read the scene chiefly as Peter's restoration after his denial: forgiven, he is given back his calling as an apostle and pastor. They note that every pastor is told to feed the flock (1 Peter 5:2), and that the text says nothing of successors.

All agree on much. Peter failed, and Jesus restored him. Love for Jesus shows itself in care for his people. And the sheep are always Christ's own. These notes do not decide between the readings.
passages.asks:
This passage is for anyone who has failed Jesus and wonders whether they can come back. Peter had denied him three times, with oaths, on the worst night of Jesus' life. Jesus did not ask him to explain himself, or to promise never to fail again. He asked one question: ‘Do you love Me?’ Then he gave him work.

If you have walked away, or denied him in your words or your life, the way back is the same. Not a speech, not a probation, but an honest answer to that one question, and then the next thing he gives you to do. Peter's last answer is a good one to borrow: ‘Lord, You know all things. You know I love You.’ He knows the failure. He knows the love, too.

passages.t: When you are old, and Follow Me
passages.happening:
Jesus goes on: “Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go” (verse 18).

John explains: “Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God.” Then Jesus says to him, “Follow Me” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Peter had said at the supper, ‘Lord, why can't I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You’ (13:37). Jesus had answered, “Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later” (13:36). Now ‘later’ is named. Peter will follow Jesus all the way, to death.

‘Stretch out your hands’ was heard by many early Christian readers as a picture of crucifixion, the arms stretched on the beam, and John's own comment says the words pointed to how Peter would die. John uses the same phrase he used of Jesus' death: the kind of death by which he would glorify God (compare 12:33, 18:32).

How did Peter die? The New Testament does not tell the story. 2 Peter has the apostle say his death is near, “as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me” (2 Peter 1:14). Clement of Rome, writing to the church at Corinth late in the first century, speaks of Peter enduring many labors and bearing witness to the end, without saying how he died. Later writers are more definite. The church historian Eusebius, in the early 300s, says that Peter was crucified at Rome under the emperor Nero, and he reports Origen's account that Peter asked to be crucified head downward. This is early and widely held tradition. It is not told in Scripture, and it should be called tradition.

Then the two words Jesus first said to Peter by the lake, years before: ‘Follow Me’.
passages.ot: Old age in the Scriptures is often a time of weakness, when others must help: “Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails” (Psalm 71:9). Jesus tells Peter honestly that his life will end in someone else's hands. But a psalm also says of the righteous, “In old age they will still bear fruit” (Psalm 92:14). Peter's death, too, will be fruitful. It will glorify God.
passages.hard:
Did Jesus tell Peter his future so that he would live in dread of it? John does not present it that way. The man who, only a short time before, could not face a servant girl's question is told that he will one day face death for Jesus, and face it well. It is a promise of courage as much as a warning of suffering. The Peter of Acts, preaching openly in Jerusalem (Acts 4:13, 19-20), shows a man already changed.

This passage is not a promise that every faithful Christian will die a martyr, nor a call to seek suffering. Most of Jesus' followers have not been killed for him. It is a promise that he goes ahead of his people even into the places they fear most.
passages.asks: When Peter was young, he went where he wanted. Jesus told him that one day he would be led where he did not want to go, and that this, too, would glorify God. Ask where your life is going that you did not choose, through age, illness or circumstance. And hear the two words Jesus gave Peter for every stage of life, young and old: ‘Follow Me.’

passages.t: What is that to you? You follow Me
passages.happening:
Peter turns and sees the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who had leaned back against Jesus at the supper and asked who would betray him (verse 20). “Lord, what about him?” Peter asks (verse 21).

Jesus answers, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!” (verse 22).

So a rumor spreads among the believers that this disciple would not die. But Jesus did not say that. He said only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Peter has just heard hard news about his own future, and his first thought is to ask about someone else's. It is a very human question. Jesus' answer is gentle but firm: that is not your business. Your business is to follow me.

The rumor in verse 23 tells us something about the people who first read this book. They believed that the beloved disciple would live until Jesus came back. John corrects them carefully, quoting Jesus' exact words. The book page notes that this may mean the disciple had died by the time the chapter was written. If so, his friends wanted no one's faith shaken by it. If so, the ‘we’ of verse 24 are the people who knew him, setting the record straight.
passages.ot: The prophet Micah says, “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Each person is answerable for his own walk with God. Ezekiel says it too: each person answers to God for his own life (Ezekiel 18:20). Jesus says the same thing to Peter: ‘You follow Me.’
passages.hard:
Did Jesus promise that the beloved disciple would live until he returned? No, and John takes care to say so. Jesus said ‘if I want’; it was a ‘what if’, not a promise. The early believers made it into a promise, and the chapter corrects them.

This has a lesson for how Christians read Scripture. A saying of Jesus can be stretched into something he never said, and passed on until many believe it. The cure is the one John uses: go back to the exact words. ‘Jesus did not say that he would not die, but only...’
passages.asks: ‘What is that to you? You follow Me.’ Ask whose life you have been comparing with your own: someone with an easier road, more gifts, a longer life, fewer losses. Jesus does not explain why his paths differ. He tells each of us the same thing: you follow me. Your road is yours, and he walks it with you.

passages.t: This is the disciple who testifies
passages.happening:
“This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true” (verse 24).

“There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The book ends by telling us where it comes from. The beloved disciple is the witness behind it, and he has ‘written them down’, whether with his own hand or by having them written. Then a group speaks up: ‘we know that his testimony is true’.

The book page explains, in ‘Who wrote it, and how we know’, what this means. The book claims to rest on an eyewitness, and a circle of people around him vouches for him. From the late second century the church named him John, the son of Zebedee. Others think he was a disciple from Jerusalem who was not one of the Twelve. Nearly every view agrees that the book rests on the memory of someone who was there.

The last verse changes from ‘we’ to ‘I’. Someone, perhaps the one who put the book into its final form, adds a personal word: ‘I suppose’. It is the friendly overstatement of someone who has known far more stories than he could write.
passages.ot:
The law of Moses said that a matter must be settled by witnesses: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). John's book is built on witness from start to finish: John the Baptist, the Samaritan woman, the works of Jesus, the Father, the Scriptures, the Spirit, the disciples. Now the last witness is named, and others stand beside him.

And the end of the book reaches back to the beginning. It began, ‘In the beginning was the Word’, the Word through whom the world was made (1:1-3). It ends by saying that the world could not hold all that he did. The world he made is too small for the story of what he has done.
passages.hard:
Who are the ‘we’? John does not say. Many think they are the disciple's own circle, the church that knew him and finished the book after his death, as the rumor in verse 23 may suggest. Others think the writer is speaking of himself and his readers together. The book page sets out the views fairly. Whichever is right, the claim is the same: this is not legend from far away, but testimony from people who knew the witness and stood behind his word.

And does ‘many more things’ mean the Gospels left out what matters most? No. John has already told us why he wrote what he did (20:31). He chose. He did not tell everything. He told enough for you to believe and to have life.
passages.asks: John's book ends with a witness, a group who stood by him, and the honest admission that there was far more to tell. Ask what you will do with the testimony you have now read, from the Word in the beginning to breakfast on the shore. Then ask what part of his story you will tell. The books the world could not hold are still being written, in the lives of people who follow him.
